abstract: |
  A four-dimensional Hawkes process fitted to the price moves of the Binance BTC perpetual and spot markets gives a closed-form forecast of the basis a few seconds ahead. Fitted on one four-hour window and applied to the next, the forecast earns $0.4$--$1.3\,\mathrm{bp}$ per round trip when both legs are filled at the mid and $0.1$--$0.7\,\mathrm{bp}$ when they are filled at the best quotes ($0.44\,\mathrm{bp}$ on average over ten BTC days), positive on all twelve trading days of the sample and stable for latencies up to about ten milliseconds. A naive lead--lag rule that looks better at the mid is destroyed at the touch by adverse selection. The touch costs the Hawkes signal more than the average spread would suggest, because at the instant of a decision the spread of the leg that has just moved is two to three times its average. Round-trip fees on Binance range from $2.2\,\mathrm{bp}$ for a top-tier maker to $30\,\mathrm{bp}$ for a regular taker, and no signal covers them. A conservative bound on maker execution shows that posting passively loses as well. The forecast is statistically significant and economically worthless at these costs.
number-sections: true
number-depth: 3

# The question

On Binance, the BTCUSDT perpetual and the BTCUSDT spot pair trade on the same venue, and their difference, the basis, fluctuates by about one basis point around a slowly moving level. The perpetual usually moves first and the spot follows within milliseconds to a second. A model that captures this mutual excitation should be able to say, at any instant, whether the basis is more likely to rise or fall in the next few seconds. This article reports what happens when that forecast is turned into a trading rule and taken through the spread, the latency and the fees of the exchange. The forecast works. The trade does not pay.

The data are the best bid and offer streams of both instruments on the first day of the month for ten BTC days between December 2022 and September 2026, plus two ETH days used as an out-of-sample check. An *event* is a move of the mid-price of either leg by at least half a basis point of a reference price, signed up or down. This gives four event types: perpetual up, perpetual down, spot up, spot down.

# The forecast in one page

Each event type $i$ has an intensity, the instantaneous rate at which it occurs. In a linear Hawkes model with exponential kernels the intensity is a baseline plus the decaying influence of every past event, $$\lambda_i(t) = \mu_i(t) + \sum_{j}\sum_{k=1}^{2} x_{ijk}(t), \qquad
x_{ijk}(t) = \alpha_{ijk} \sum_{t^j_n < t} e^{-\beta_{ijk}(t - t^j_n)},$$ where $x_{ijk}$ is the contribution of past events of type $j$ to type $i$ through the $k$-th of two exponentials, one fast (milliseconds) and one slow (fractions of a second). The baseline $\mu_i(t)$ is piecewise constant on fifteen-minute bins to absorb intraday seasonality. The fitted model is dominated by cross-excitation: a perpetual up-move raises the rate of spot up-moves more than it raises the rate of further perpetual up-moves, so the basis tends to close by imitation between the legs.

The vector $x(t)$ is a Markov state. Its expected evolution is linear, $\frac{d}{ds}\mathbb{E}[x(s)\mid\mathcal{F}_t] = A\,\mathbb{E}[x(s)\mid\mathcal{F}_t] + b$, with a generator $A$ built from the decays and the excitation coefficients and $b_{ijk} = \alpha_{ijk}\mu_j$. Integrating gives the expected number of events of each type over a horizon $h$ in closed form ([Bacry 2015](#ref-bacry2015)): 

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[N(t+h) - N(t) \,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_t\big] = \mu h + C\big(I_h\, x(t) + J_h\, b\big),
\qquad I_h = \int_0^h e^{Au}\,du, \quad J_h = \int_0^h I_u\,du,
$$ {#eq-forecast}

 where $C$ sums the contributions of each type and $I_h$, $J_h$ come from one exponential of a block matrix built from $A$. The basis is a linear functional of the counts, $B(t) = B(0) + v_B^\top N(t)$ with $v_B = (m_p, -m_p, -m_s, m_s)$ and $m_p$, $m_s$ the mean event sizes of the two legs. The trading signal is the forecast change of the basis in excess of its unconditional drift $v_B^\top \Lambda h$, with $\Lambda$ the stationary intensities: 

$$
s_h(t) = v_B^\top\, \mathbb{E}\big[N(t+h) - N(t) \,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_t\big] - v_B^\top \Lambda\, h .
$$ {#eq-signal}

 A positive $s_h$ says that the recent events, through the fitted kernels, are expected to generate more perpetual up-moves and spot down-moves than the reverse over the next $h$ seconds. Nothing in @eq-signal is fitted to profits: it is a by-product of the maximum-likelihood fit of the kernels. Horizons of $1$, $3$ and $10$ s are computed; the main configuration uses $h = 10$ s.

# How the backtest avoids look-ahead

Every quantity used at time $t$ is computed from information available at $t$.

#### Walk-forward by window.

Each day is cut into six windows of four hours starting at 00:00 UTC. The Hawkes model is estimated on each window separately. The parameters of window $w-1$ generate the signal on window $w$, for $w = 1,\dots,5$, so nothing estimated on a window is used on that window. The marks in $v_B$ are the mean event sizes of the events that precede the decision window.

#### State.

The state $x(t)$ is accumulated from the start of the day through all events up to and including the one at $t$, with the parameters of the previous window. This uses only past events and avoids an artificial empty history at the start of each trading window.

#### Rule.

One unit of basis is traded. If flat and $s > \theta_{\mathrm{in}}$, buy the basis (long perpetual, short spot); if $s < -\theta_{\mathrm{in}}$, sell it. An open position is reversed when the signal exceeds the threshold with the opposite sign, closed when $|s| < \theta_{\mathrm{in}}/3$ and the position is at least one second old, and closed in any case after sixty seconds. The thresholds $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5\}\,\mathrm{bp}$ and the horizons form a fixed grid; nothing is optimised, and the main configuration is $h = 10$ s, $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{bp}$.

#### Execution.

Decision times are the events of the decision window, the same for every signal. An order decided at $t$ reaches the market at $t + \ell$ and is filled at the quotes prevailing at that instant, for both entry and exit, with a latency $\ell \in \{0, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100\}$ ms. At the *mid* both legs fill at their mid-quotes and no spread is paid: this measures the signal as a forecast and is an upper bound on any execution. At the *touch* a long basis buys the perpetual ask against the spot bid and sells at the perpetual bid against the spot ask, so both spreads are paid at their actual value at the fill time. The displayed quote is assumed available for the full unit: queue position and fail-to-fill are not modelled, which makes the touch itself an optimistic price ([Albers and Cucuringu 2025](#ref-albers2025)).

#### Benchmarks.

Two rules share the same decision times and the same entry and exit logic. An Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (OU) forecast uses only the level of the basis and its speed of reversion, re-estimated on the previous window. A naive lead--lag rule uses no estimation: after a perpetual move of size $m$ it bets that the basis closes by $m/2$, after a spot move that it reopens by $m/2$. It is the latency arbitrageur of ([Budish 2015](#ref-budish2015)) in its simplest form.

All profits below are in basis points of the spot price per round trip and are *gross of fees* unless a fee is stated explicitly.

# Gross results

At the mid, the Hawkes forecast at $h = 10$ s earns between $0.4$ and $1.3\,\mathrm{bp}$ per round trip on every day, over $300$ to $7\,900$ trades per day. At the touch it earns between $0.1$ and $0.7\,\mathrm{bp}$, with a mean of $0.44\,\mathrm{bp}$ over the ten BTC days and $+0.68$ and $+0.25\,\mathrm{bp}$ on the two ETH days, so it is positive on all twelve days. Hit rates at the touch lie between $0.56$ and $0.81$. The $t$-statistic of the mean exceeds $7$ on eight BTC days and is $4.8$ and $2.3$ on the two days with the least left at the touch (1 February 2023, the day with the widest spreads, and 1 May 2025). These are out-of-sample numbers, and the sample includes three days in Binance's zero-fee spot promotion on which price leadership is reversed and the spot leads; the signal learns the direction from the previous window and stays positive there ($+0.48$, $+0.10$ and $+0.69\,\mathrm{bp}$).

@fig-cumpnl shows one day. Both the Hawkes and the OU rule accumulate steadily from 04:00 to midnight. The naive rule, not drawn because it would compress the scale, ends the same day at about $-10\,600\,\mathrm{bp}$.

![BTC, 1 March 2026, cumulative gross profit at the touch, latency zero, windows 1--5. The OU rule trades about three times more often than the Hawkes rule at a similar profit per trade. The naive lead--lag rule (not shown) ends the day at about $-10\,600\,\mathrm{bp}$.](figures/diagram-1.svg){#fig-cumpnl}

Two comparisons qualify the result. The OU forecast, which knows the level of the basis but not the event history, does a little better: $+0.94\,\mathrm{bp}$ at the mid and $+0.57\,\mathrm{bp}$ at the touch on average over BTC at $h = 3$ s, positive on all ten days, ahead of the Hawkes rule by $0.13\,\mathrm{bp}$ per trade. At the scale of a few seconds the level carries more usable information than the recent sequence of events, which is consistent with the linear Hawkes model reverting the basis more slowly than the data do. The naive lead--lag rule is the instructive case. At the mid it earns $+1.07\,\mathrm{bp}$ on average and beats the Hawkes signal on seven BTC days out of ten. At the touch it loses $0.85\,\mathrm{bp}$ on BTC and $0.91$ and $2.76\,\mathrm{bp}$ on the two ETH days, and is negative on ten days out of twelve. The quote it wants to hit is the stale quote of the lagging leg, and the price at which it can actually trade sits on the far side of a spread that has just widened. This is the adverse selection of latency arbitrage ([Budish 2015](#ref-budish2015); [Albers and Cucuringu 2025](#ref-albers2025)): whoever is faster takes the stale quote, and the slower trader gets the fills that lose.

# Where the edge goes

## The spread at decision time

Moving from the mid to the touch costs the Hawkes signal $0.40\,\mathrm{bp}$ per round trip on BTC (from $+0.84$ to $+0.44\,\mathrm{bp}$). The unconditional cost of crossing both spreads once, averaged over all quote changes of a day, is only $0.08$--$0.26\,\mathrm{bp}$. The difference comes from timing. The signal trades at events, and at an event the leg that has just moved has a transiently wide spread. On 1 March 2026, for example, the cost of crossing both legs is $0.14\,\mathrm{bp}$ over all quote changes and $0.36\,\mathrm{bp}$ at the decision events; across days the cost at decision time is two to three times its average. A backtest that charges the average spread would overstate this strategy.

## Latency

@fig-frontier shows the latency frontier. At the mid every signal loses value with latency, and the naive rule loses it fastest ($+1.07$ to $+0.34\,\mathrm{bp}$ between zero and one hundred milliseconds): the information in a stale quote disappears once the quote updates. At the touch the frontier is not monotone. The Hawkes profit rises from $+0.44$ to $+0.56\,\mathrm{bp}$ between zero and one millisecond and stays near that level up to ten milliseconds before declining to $+0.36\,\mathrm{bp}$ at one hundred, still positive on nine of ten BTC days. The spread that must be crossed narrows by a third within one millisecond of the event and by a half within ten, faster than the forecast decays. This rise depends on the displayed quote still being there when the order arrives, which is exactly what ([Albers and Cucuringu 2025](#ref-albers2025)) find to fail in these moments, so the touch frontier is an upper bound on profit.

![Latency frontier: gross profit per round trip against the delay between the decision event and the fill, mean over the ten BTC days. Hawkes $h = 10$ s, $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} = 0.5$; OU $h = 3$ s, $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} = 0.3$; naive lead--lag $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} = 0.5$. Solid lines at the touch, dashed at the mid. The horizontal axis is categorical.](figures/diagram-2.svg){#fig-frontier}

## Fees

Binance charges each fill a share of the notional, by account tier and by side. A round trip on the basis is four fills, two per leg. Under the schedule in force in October 2026 it costs $30\,\mathrm{bp}$ for a regular account taking liquidity on both legs, $8\,\mathrm{bp}$ at the highest VIP tier as taker, and $2.2\,\mathrm{bp}$ at the highest tier as maker on both legs. @tbl-costs subtracts these fees from the gross profit at the touch.

No signal covers the fees of a regular account, by more than an order of magnitude, and none covers the taker fees of the top tier. The best gross profits at the touch, $0.44\,\mathrm{bp}$ for Hawkes and $0.57\,\mathrm{bp}$ for OU, are about a quarter of the cheapest round trip on the schedule. The OU rule at $h = 1$ s comes closest, at $-0.03\,\mathrm{bp}$ with the $2.2\,\mathrm{bp}$ fee, but it fires only on the largest excursions of the basis: between $13$ and $2\,400$ trades per BTC day, fewer than thirty on two days. Raising the entry threshold does not help: from $\theta_{\mathrm{in}} = 0.1$ to $0.5\,\mathrm{bp}$ the Hawkes profit per trade rises from $0.08$ to $0.44\,\mathrm{bp}$ while the number of trades falls by a factor of seven. The same picture, profitable at zero fees and unprofitable at retail fees, is reported by ([He and Manela 2022](#ref-he2022)) for lead--lag strategies across crypto exchanges.

## The maker bound

The $2.2\,\mathrm{bp}$ column applies the maker fee to fills at the touch, but a maker does not trade at the touch. A resting order joins a queue and tends to be filled when the market moves against it. Pricing this properly needs a queue model and book depth, which the quote streams used here do not carry. They do allow a bound. In the *fill-on-cross* rule a resting buy at the bid is filled only when the ask falls to the bid price or below, and a resting sell at the ask only when the bid rises to it. At that point the market has traded through the level and every order resting there has been executed, whatever its queue position. Fills by queue depletion without a cross are ignored, so the rule understates the fill rate.

The rule is applied to the same signals. At a decision both legs are posted at the touch; each fills when crossed within a window of $3$ or $10$ s. Once the first leg fills, the second is given a hedge delay of $0$, $1$ or $10$ s, and if still unfilled it is completed as a taker. Exits follow the same procedure. Fees are charged per leg at the top tier: $0$ and $1.7\,\mathrm{bp}$ per fill on the perpetual as maker and taker, $1.1$ and $2.3\,\mathrm{bp}$ on the spot. @tbl-maker gives the Hawkes rows.

Fill window and hedge delay in seconds; completed round trips; share of entries with both legs filled as maker and of round trips with all four legs as maker; gross profit per round trip (bp) over all round trips, the all-maker ones and those with at least one taker leg; net at the top VIP tier with fees per leg, BTC mean and ETH mean. The net is negative on every day.
:::

With a ten-second window and a ten-second hedge delay, a third of the entries get both legs crossed and $16\%$ of the round trips are filled as maker on all four legs. Those round trips earn about $+0.9\,\mathrm{bp}$: the half basis point of the taker analysis plus the two spreads a maker does not pay. The round trips with at least one taker leg lose $3.4\,\mathrm{bp}$ on average, an order of magnitude more than the spread, and they are the majority. The mechanism is the one described by ([Albers and Cucuringu 2025](#ref-albers2025)). The two legs move together. After a common move of the price, the leg posted on the wrong side of the move is crossed and filled at its stale price, while the leg on the right side is not. The maker is left holding one leg of a basis that has moved against it by the size of the move, and the hedge at the end of the delay locks the loss in. Hedging immediately removes the legging loss (gross $+0.11\,\mathrm{bp}$) but pays two taker legs per round trip, for a net of $-5.0\,\mathrm{bp}$ at the top tier. No configuration is positive net of fees on any of the twelve days, for any of the three signals.

The profitable all-maker round trips are identified after the fact. They are the attempts in which the market moved as predicted and crossed both legs from the right side. A trader cannot select them in advance, and the attempts in which the market moved the other way are exactly the ones that get filled on one leg only. The bound is pessimistic in one respect: it ignores fills by queue depletion in a quiet book, which are the fills real market makers live on. A queue model estimated on depth data could recover part of them; whether enough to change the sign is open.

# The lesson

The Hawkes forecast is a genuine out-of-sample predictor of the basis. Its $t$-statistics are large, it is positive on every day, and it survives latencies that a co-located participant can achieve. It is worth about half a basis point per round trip at the touch, after both spreads have been paid at their value at the fill time. That half basis point is a quarter of the cheapest round-trip fee on Binance, and as a maker it is lost to fills on the wrong side of common moves. Statistical significance measures whether a forecast contains information. Tradability depends on whether that information exceeds the cost of acting on it at the moment it appears, and for this signal it does not.

The exercise also says something about backtests of short-horizon signals. A backtest at the mid says little about them, and a backtest at the touch is still optimistic if it charges the average spread instead of the spread at the decision instant. A rule that hits stale quotes looks best at the mid and worst at the touch. A maker backtest that keeps the round trips filled on both legs and forgets the ones filled on one leg selects on the outcome.

This article is a research report on historical data and is not a trading recommendation.
